marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q001.takeaway: The bare area of the liver is related to the abdominal esophagus on its posterior surface in the marked region.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q001.displayText:
The bare area of the liver is related to the abdominal esophagus on its posterior surface in the marked region.

The area marked 'A' on the posterior surface of the liver is related to the esophagus.

The source figure shows the visceral/posterior impressions of the liver, including esophageal, gastric, suprarenal, renal, duodenal and colic impressions.
emphasis: The bare area of the liver is related to the abdominal esophagus on its posterior surface in the marked region

rationales.a: Aorta lies posterior to the liver but is not the structure at this specific upper visceral impression.
rationales.c: Duodenum impressions lie on the inferior visceral surface.
rationales.d: Pylorus is inferior and related to the visceral surface, not the marked posterior area.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q002.takeaway: Couinaud segments are divided by portal-vein branches and portal pedicles; hepatic veins mark intersegmental planes.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q002.displayText:
Couinaud segments are divided by portal-vein branches and portal pedicles; hepatic veins mark intersegmental planes.

Couinaud's segments are divided based on the distribution of the portal vein.

Veins of the liver: the portal vein collects blood from the gall bladder, pancreas, spleen, and abdominal part of the alimentary tract and transfers blood collected from these organs to the liver. Hepatic veins collect deoxygenated blood from the liver and drain directly into the inferior vena cava and ultimately into the heart.

Note: Left hemihepatectomy involves resection of segments II, III, and IV. Right hemihepatectomy involves resection of segments V, VI, VII, and VIII.
emphasis: Couinaud segments are divided by portal-vein branches and portal pedicles; hepatic veins mark intersegmental planes

rationales.a: Hepatic artery branches accompany portal branches but do not define segment boundaries.
rationales.c: Bile ducts accompany portal triads and drain segments; portal venous territories define Couinaud units.
rationales.d: Hepatic veins run between segments, rather than forming the functional segmental inflow units.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q003.takeaway: The cholecysto-caval (Cantlie) line runs from gallbladder fossa to IVC and separates functional right and left liver.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q003.displayText:
The cholecysto-caval (Cantlie) line runs from gallbladder fossa to IVC and separates functional right and left liver.

The cholecysto-vena caval line (Cantlie line) separates the right and left lobe of the liver.

Cantlie line is an imaginary line that divides the liver into two planes. It extends from the midpoint of the gallbladder fossa at the inferior margin of the liver back to the midpoint of the inferior vena cava and contains the middle hepatic vein.
emphasis: The cholecysto-caval (Cantlie) line runs from gallbladder fossa to IVC and separates functional right and left liver

rationales.a: The line does not simply divide gallbladder from IVC; those mark its endpoints.
rationales.b: Porta hepatis and IVC are not the structures separated by this plane.
rationales.c: Caudate and quadrate lobes are not separated by Cantlie line.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q004.displayText:
The right hemiliver contains Couinaud segments V, VI, VII and VIII.

The right part of the liver includes Couinaud's segments V, VI, VII, and VIII.

The given CT abdomen shows a large cystic lesion in the right lobe, presumed in the source explanation to occur due to appendicitis.

rationales.b: This omits segment VIII, a right anterior-superior segment.
rationales.c: Segment IV belongs to the left medial section, not the right liver.
rationales.d: This omits segment V, a right anterior-inferior segment.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q005.takeaway: Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells are label 3 and store vitamin A in the space of Disse.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q005.displayText:
Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells are label 3 and store vitamin A in the space of Disse.

Ito cells, or hepatic stellate cells, are marked as 3 in the histological image and store vitamin A. They are present in the space of Disse and are mesenchymal in origin.

They have two states. In the dormant state, they store the fat-soluble vitamin A in lipid droplets and are a significant source of growth factors involved in liver homeostasis and regeneration. In the active state, after liver injury they replace damaged hepatocytes with collagenous scar tissue leading to hepatic fibrosis and secrete intralobular matrix components including collagen type III (reticular) fibres.

The space of Disse lies between a hepatocyte and a sinusoid. It contains interstitial fluid, microvilli of adjacent hepatocytes and fine collagen fibres (mostly type III). Lymph produced in the liver drains through the perisinusoidal space of Disse and periportal clefts of Mall into larger lymphatics.
emphasis: Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells are label 3 and store vitamin A in the space of Disse

rationales.a: Label 1 is another sinusoidal/lobular cell, not the vitamin-A-storing stellate cell.
rationales.b: Label 2 is not the Ito cell identified by its perisinusoidal position.
rationales.d: Label 4 is not the stellate cell marked in the source histology.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q006.takeaway: Couinaud segment IV is the left medial segment; the caudate lobe is segment I, making statement IV false.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q006.displayText:
Couinaud segment IV is the left medial segment; the caudate lobe is segment I, making statement IV false.

Segment IV (left medial sector) corresponds to the quadrate lobe and not the caudate lobe (segment I). It is part of the physiological left lobe of liver (segments II, III, and IV) and is drained by the left hepatic duct.

The physiological left lobe is supplied by the left hepatic duct and left branch of the portal vein. The physiological right lobe (segments V, VI, VII, and VIII) is drained by the right hepatic duct and supplied by the right hepatic artery and right branch of the portal vein.

About 80% of blood supply to the liver is through the portal vein whereas 20% is through the hepatic artery.

Pringle's manoeuvre is compression of the hepatic pedicle at the free edge of the lesser omentum for rapid control of hemorrhage from vessels entering the porta hepatis. The lesser omentum can be divided immediately to the left of these structures and passing a tape around them through the epiploic foramen.
emphasis: Couinaud segment IV is the left medial segment; the caudate lobe is segment I, making statement IV false

rationales.a: Quadrate lobe is associated with left hepatic duct drainage in the source description.
rationales.b: Pringle maneuver compresses the portal triad in the free edge of lesser omentum.
rationales.c: Portal vein supplies roughly 75–80% of hepatic blood flow.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q007.takeaway: The caudate lobe can enlarge in Budd–Chiari syndrome because it drains directly into the IVC through short hepatic veins.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q007.displayText:
The caudate lobe can enlarge in Budd–Chiari syndrome because it drains directly into the IVC through short hepatic veins.

The area marked in the image is the caudate lobe of the liver. Caudate lobe hypertrophy is seen in Budd-Chiari syndrome.

This segment is unique in that it receives blood supply from both the right and left portal veins and hepatic arteries. It directly drains into the inferior vena cava.

It also forms the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
emphasis: The caudate lobe can enlarge in Budd–Chiari syndrome because it drains directly into the IVC through short hepatic veins

rationales.a: Quadrate lobe lies inferiorly on the visceral surface and is not the structure enlarged here.
rationales.c: “Middle lobe” is not the caudate structure highlighted.
rationales.d: The left lobe is not selectively enlarged by direct IVC drainage.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q008.takeaway: Hepatic veins drain into the IVC outside the porta hepatis and are least directly affected by a porta-hepatis tumor.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q008.displayText:
Hepatic veins drain into the IVC outside the porta hepatis and are least directly affected by a porta-hepatis tumor.

Hepatic veins do not enter or exit the liver at the porta hepatis and are least likely to be involved by a tumor at that location.

Porta hepatis is a deep transverse fissure on the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver. Structures entering the porta hepatis include portal vein, hepatic artery, and hepatic nervous plexus. Structures exiting include right and left hepatic bile ducts and lymphatics.

The classical features of portal hypertension are ascites, splenomegaly, esophageal varices, and distended veins around the umbilicus.
emphasis: Hepatic veins drain into the IVC outside the porta hepatis and are least directly affected by a porta-hepatis tumor

rationales.a: Hepatic artery passes through the porta hepatis in the hepatoduodenal ligament.
rationales.b: Hepatic nerve plexus follows the hepatic artery into porta hepatis.
rationales.d: Hepatic ducts pass through porta hepatis and may be compressed by tumor.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q009.takeaway: The Valoean (Glissonian) sheath encloses portal triad branches—portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct—in the liver.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q009.displayText:
The Valoean (Glissonian) sheath encloses portal triad branches—portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct—in the liver.

The fibrous sheath surrounding the hepatic artery, bile duct, and portal vein in each liver segment is referred to as Valoean sheath.

This is an extension of Glisson's capsule, which becomes condensed as a sheath around the branches of the portal triad structures as they enter the liver parenchyma. This arrangement facilitates surgical control of the right and left vasculo-biliary pedicles of the liver.
emphasis: The Valoean (Glissonian) sheath encloses portal triad branches—portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct—in the liver

rationales.a: The gallbladder has its own serosa/connective tissue, not the segmental portal triad sheath.
rationales.b: Splenic hilar vessels are not enclosed by the hepatic Glisson sheath.
rationales.d: The ampullary region has sphincteric tissue, not the segmental hepatic sheath.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q010.takeaway: Hartmann pouch is an outpouching near the gallbladder neck that may contain a stone.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q010.displayText:
Hartmann pouch is an outpouching near the gallbladder neck that may contain a stone.

Hartmann's pouch is seen in the gallbladder.

Hartmann's pouch (infundibulum) is an outpouching at the junction of the neck of the gallbladder and the cystic duct. Although frequently seen, it is not a constant feature of the gallbladder and serves as a potential space where gallstones can lodge.

Option A: Pouch of Douglas or recto-uterine pouch is the most dependent part of the abdomen in the erect position in females. Option B: Rathke's pouch is an ectodermal outpouching from the developing pharynx that gives rise to the anterior pituitary. Option C: Morison's pouch or hepatorenal pouch is the most dependent part of the abdomen in the supine position and pathological fluid may collect there.
emphasis: Hartmann pouch is an outpouching near the gallbladder neck that may contain a stone

rationales.a: Pouch of Douglas is the rectouterine/rectovesical peritoneal pouch.
rationales.b: Rathke pouch is an embryologic pituitary structure.
rationales.c: Morison pouch is the hepatorenal recess.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q011.takeaway: The cystic artery usually branches from the right hepatic artery within the hepatobiliary triangle.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q011.displayText:
The cystic artery usually branches from the right hepatic artery within the hepatobiliary triangle.

The marked structure is the cystic artery. It is a branch of the right hepatic artery.

The cystic artery is the main source of blood supply to the biliary system. After originating from the right hepatic artery, it passes posterior to the common hepatic duct and superior to the cystic duct at the hepatobiliary triangle. On reaching the superior aspect of the neck of the gallbladder, it divides into superficial and deep branches.
emphasis: The cystic artery usually branches from the right hepatic artery within the hepatobiliary triangle

rationales.a: Proper hepatic artery divides into right and left hepatic arteries; the cystic artery usually branches from right hepatic.
rationales.c: SMA is not the normal cystic artery source.
rationales.d: Common hepatic artery usually gives gastroduodenal then continues as proper hepatic; cystic artery arises from right hepatic.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q012.takeaway: Spiral valves of Heister in the cystic duct can impede catheter passage during cholangiography.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q012.displayText:
Spiral valves of Heister in the cystic duct can impede catheter passage during cholangiography.

Spiral valves of Heister are the mucosal folds present in the cystic duct. In most cases, they are responsible for causing difficulty in the passage of a catheter through the cystic duct.

The mucosa of the cystic duct forms 2-10 crescentic folds which are spirally arranged to form the spiral valve of Heister, also called spiral folds. These are continuous with those in the neck of the gallbladder. The function of these spiral folds is unknown but they may help to preserve the patency of this narrow, tortuous duct.

The cystic duct drains the gallbladder into the common hepatic duct. It unites with the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct.

Note: Tortuous course of the right hepatic artery, also known as Moynihan's hump or caterpillar hump, is a rare but important anomaly to recognize to prevent intraoperative vascular and biliary injuries during surgical procedures involving the liver and biliary apparatus.
emphasis: Spiral valves of Heister in the cystic duct can impede catheter passage during cholangiography

rationales.a: Moynihan hump describes tortuous right hepatic artery, not the valve folds in cystic duct.
rationales.b: An anomalous hepatic duct can complicate cannulation but the characteristic obstruction is Heister valves.
rationales.d: Tortuosity can make passage harder, but the source asks the internal spiral folds.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q013.takeaway: The gallbladder is not a boundary of Calot’s triangle; the classic boundaries are cystic duct, common hepatic duct and cystic artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q013.displayText:
The gallbladder is not a boundary of Calot’s triangle; the classic boundaries are cystic duct, common hepatic duct and cystic artery.

The gall bladder does not form a boundary of Calot's triangle.

Calot's triangle is bounded by the three Cs: medially by the common hepatic duct, inferiorly by the cystic duct, and superiorly by the cystic artery.
emphasis: The gallbladder is not a boundary of Calot’s triangle; the classic boundaries are cystic duct, common hepatic duct and cystic artery

rationales.a: Common hepatic duct forms the medial boundary.
rationales.b: Cystic duct forms the inferior/lateral boundary.
rationales.c: Cystic artery traverses the triangle and is included in the classic boundaries.

marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q014.takeaway: Left lower rib fractures with hemoperitoneum threaten the spleen beneath ribs 9–11 on the left.
marrow__ANAT_CH50_Q014.displayText:
Left lower rib fractures with hemoperitoneum threaten the spleen beneath ribs 9–11 on the left.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of injury to the spleen.

The spleen is a wedge-shaped organ and extends from the 10th rib to the 12th rib in the left hypochondrium. It lies along the long axis of the 11th rib and is likely to be injured in blunt trauma to the abdomen. Laceration of the spleen leads to profuse intra-abdominal bleeding and hypovolemic shock.

It is not palpable in a normal adult. For the spleen to be palpable, it has to become about three times its normal size.

Source note: The explanation notes anatomical variation in rib relation; some sources mention the 9th to 11th ribs, while Gray's Anatomy is cited as mentioning the 10th to 12th ribs.
emphasis: Left lower rib fractures with hemoperitoneum threaten the spleen beneath ribs 9–11 on the left

rationales.a: Pancreas is more central/retroperitoneal and not the classic left rib-associated organ.
rationales.c: Left kidney is posterior and partly protected, but spleen is the classic vulnerable organ beneath these ribs.
rationales.d: Liver lies predominantly on the right side.
